title: How to work a lazy daisy in cross-stitch
subtitle: The looped petal stitch for small flowers and leaf shapes
excerpt: A lazy daisy is a single petal-shaped loop anchored at its tip. Each loop is worked independently from the same central hole, and a cluster of five or six loops around a French-knot centre makes a small flower. It is one of the mixed-media stitches that appear in floral cross-stitch charts alongside the counted fill.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776. The lazy daisy (also called detached chain stitch) is documented in all major Victorian embroidery references.

glossaryTerms.definition: A single petal-shaped loop of thread anchored at its tip with a small straight stitch. Several lazy daisies arranged around a centre hole make a simple flower or a leaf cluster. Also called detached chain stitch.

content.text: A
lazy daisy
is one looped petal anchored at its tip. The loop rises from the fabric and back down to a point, forming a petal or leaf shape. Six lazy daisies arranged around a
French-knot centre
make a small daisy. In a cross-stitch piece, lazy daisies appear as embellishments on the surface of the
cross-stitch fill
, where a purely counted stitch cannot produce the same organic shape.
Working a single petal
Come up at the base of the petal.
Bring the needle up through the fabric at the point where all the petals will originate, the flower centre.
Loop the thread and push the needle back in beside the same hole.
Hold a loop of thread against the fabric surface. Push the needle down into the same hole or one thread beside it, leaving the loop on the front. The needle now sits below the fabric.
Come up at the petal tip, inside the loop.
Bring the needle up at the point where the petal tip will sit, passing through the loop of thread before pulling through. The loop is now caught around the needle.
Pull the loop snug and anchor it.
Pull the thread through until the loop sits as a petal shape on the fabric surface. Push the needle down just beyond the tip of the loop to make a tiny anchor stitch that holds the petal in place.
Repeat for each petal.
Come up again at the centre hole and rotate the angle for the next petal. Petals arranged evenly around the centre point form a round flower.
Getting the size right

The petal length is controlled by how far from the centre the tip sits. For most cross-stitch pieces, a petal of four to six Aida squares in length sits in proportion to the counted fill. Longer petals droop unless stitched in a stiffer single strand; two strands give a firmer loop.
